newsitem.title: COTE D'IVOIRE: Ivory Coast shipyard strike enters tenth day.
newsitem.headline: Ivory Coast shipyard strike enters tenth day.

text.p: A pay strike paralysing Ivory Coast's French-owned ship building and repair firm CARENA entered its tenth day after workers refused to return to work on Friday, a spokesman said on Friday.
Offshore oil and gas operators, CARENA's main clients, said the strike had not had any impact.
The Ivorian ship builders' and repairers' union SYLICORENA is demanding pay in line with naval repair and construction trades instead of mechanical industry rates.
CARENA began a "lock-out" of its workers on Monday but none had returned to work on Friday when the ban was lifted, said a the spokesman.
CARENA services the offshore oil and gas exploration sector along with fishing vessels and lagoon transport boats.

"Construction might be affected in two to three weeks -- I could go on with exploration for another two months," said a spokesman for Houston, U.S.-based United Meridian International Corporation (UMIC), the only producer of oil and gas currently operating off Ivory Coast.
"It hit us at a low so we will not really be affected. We had most of our stuff out of there already." he told Reuters.
Offshore Ivory Coast oil production of 20,000 barrels per day and gas production ranging, according to demand, between 45,000-60,000 cubic feet a day would not be affected, he added.
CARENA, owned by 50 percent shareholding French firms Bollore and Ateliers des Chantiers du Havre, employs 340 staff, with another 260 on contractual terms, including 20 expatriates.
Around eight vessels had left CARENA since the strike began but two remained, said the spokesman, who would not be named.
"(CARENA) is one of the best dry-docking facility in West Africa. It also has good machining facilites," said the UMIC spokesman.
UMIC began offshore production in Ivory Coast in April 1995. It has one oil and gas separation platform, one gas production platform and two oil and gas production platforms.
